questions.q: A writer has a picture she can't shake: an old man's empty bedroom with the clock stopped. She has no plot yet. What would Bergman's practice suggest?
choices: Drop it until she has a logline and a beat sheet
Treat the recurring image as the starting point and ask who is in that room and what has to happen for the picture to occur
Research the subject until a story appears in the facts
Turn the image into a twist ending
questions.explain: Bergman described films beginning as images or dreams that kept returning; Cries and Whispers grew from a red room with women in white whispering.

questions.q: In his introduction to Four Screenplays (1960), which art did Bergman say film most resembles?
choices: The novel, because both can enter a character's thoughts
Painting, because both are made of light and composition
Music, because both act on feeling directly and film is mainly rhythm
Theatre, because both depend on actors
questions.explain: He called the screenplay an imperfect technical basis for a film and said film is mainly rhythm, 'inhalation and exhalation in continuous sequence'.

questions.q: Persona plays Alma's long speech about Elisabet's son twice, word for word. What does the repetition do?
choices: It shows the same words landing on two faces, the listener's and then the speaker's, before merging them into one
It's a continuity error that Bergman decided to keep
It lets the audience catch dialogue they missed the first time
It marks a flashback to an earlier day
questions.explain: The first pass stays on Elisabet listening, the second on Alma speaking, and the sequence ends with half of each face combined in one image.

questions.q: Which describes a chamber film in Bergman's sense?
choices: A film shot entirely in a single unbroken take
A film built from documentary interviews
A film with many subplots braided together
A small cast, few locations and little plot, with drama coming from close pressure between people
questions.explain: The idea comes from Strindberg's 1907 chamber plays and chamber music; Through a Glass Darkly, Winter Light and The Silence apply it.

questions.q: A screenwriter's key revelation lands, and the script cuts straight to the next scene. What would Bergman's films suggest?
choices: Add a voice-over explaining what the character feels
Stay on a face, often the listener's, long enough for the moment to register
Add a musical sting so the audience knows it matters
Move the revelation to the climax
questions.explain: Bergman held close-ups far longer than most directors, as in Märta's letter in Winter Light or Charlotte listening to her daughter play in Autumn Sonata.

questions.q: Which of these did Bergman name as one of his own 'commandments' for filmmaking?
choices: Never let the audience know more than the hero
Always end with a moral lesson
Always be entertaining, as a duty to the audience
Never use music under dialogue
questions.explain: In the essay known in English as 'Each Film Is My Last', he listed being entertaining alongside obeying your artistic conscience and making each film as if it were your last.

questions.q: What's the fairest form of the 'solemnity' charge against Bergman?
choices: He became a byword for gloom and was widely parodied, though the charge overlooks comedies like Smiles of a Summer Night
He never made a comedy in his life
He refused to direct for the theatre
He only ever adapted other writers' novels
questions.explain: Parodies from De Düva to Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey played on his gloom, but Smiles of a Summer Night became Sondheim's A Little Night Music.

ideas: The great originality of cinema is that it can come close to the human face.
Film is mainly rhythm, like breathing, so it has more in common with music than with literature.
A film can begin from a recurring image, such as women in white whispering in a red room, before there is any plot.
Make each film as if it were your last, and always be entertaining.
